items.title: Why universities are rethinking written exams in the age of AI
items.originalSummary: As generative AI tools become widespread, several universities are piloting oral defenses, in-class essays and project-based portfolios to verify what students have actually learned.
items.learningSummary: Universities around the world are experimenting with new assessment formats as the use of generative AI tools spreads on campus. Instead of relying solely on take-home essays, some institutions are introducing oral defenses, in-class writing tasks and project-based portfolios that are harder to outsource. Supporters argue these methods give a more reliable picture of a student's real ability, while critics warn that they can be time-consuming and stressful for both students and staff. Educators broadly agree that the goal is not to ban technology but to redesign tasks so that AI becomes a study aid rather than a shortcut.

items.listeningText: Universities are quietly rethinking how they assess their students. With generative AI now widely available, take-home essays no longer prove what a student really understands. As a response, several institutions are piloting oral defenses, timed in-class writing and small group projects. Supporters say these formats offer a more reliable view of student learning, especially when combined with regular feedback. Critics, however, point out that they take more time to mark and can feel stressful for those who are not confident speakers. Most educators agree on one thing: the aim is not to fight technology, but to redesign assessments so that AI supports learning instead of replacing it.
